common_name: Reine des Violettes Rose (Queen of the Violets Hybrid Perpetual)

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil; Reine des Violettes is nearly thornless and can be grown as a large shrub or trained loosely as a short climber against a pillar.

directions: Plant in full sun to light afternoon shade in fertile, well-drained soil enriched with compost, and give the nearly thornless canes room to arch gracefully rather than crowding them against other shrubs. Bred by Millet-Malet in France and introduced in 1860, Reine des Violettes is a Hybrid Perpetual prized for its flat, quartered, old-rose-form blooms that open cerise-pink and mature to a striking violet-mauve unlike almost any other rose, carrying a strong, classic old-rose fragrance. It repeat-blooms through the growing season, though most heavily in spring, and its soft gray-green foliage and graceful, relatively thornless growth make it a favorite for cottage-style borders and cutting gardens. Prune lightly after the first flush to encourage further rebloom and remove any dead or crossing wood in late winter.

common_name: Madame Isaac Pereire Rose (Fragrant Bourbon Rose)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall in full sun in rich, well-drained soil against a fence or low wall if grown as a climber; Madame Isaac Pereire is a vigorous Bourbon that performs well through the humid Gulf South growing season, though it benefits from good air circulation to limit blackspot.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained, compost-enriched soil, and prune back by about a third after the main spring flush to encourage a strong repeat bloom later in the season. Bred by Garçon in France and introduced in 1881, Madame Isaac Pereire is a Bourbon rose renowned as one of the most fragrant roses ever raised, bearing very large, deeply cupped, ruffled blooms in a rich magenta-pink that release an intense, raspberry-like old-rose perfume detectable from a distance. Its vigorous, somewhat lax growth habit allows it to be kept as a large rounded shrub or trained as a short climber on a wall or pillar for extra height and better air movement through the dense foliage. Deadhead through summer to encourage the sporadic rebloom that follows its heavy spring display.

planting.note: Set out grafted or own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, arbor, or pillar in full sun with good air circulation; Climbing America repeats reliably through the Gulf South growing season but benefits from a preventive disease program or an airy site in humid summers.

directions: Plant in full sun in fertile, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, training canes as horizontally as possible along the structure to promote flowering side shoots along the entire length of the plant. Discovered as a climbing sport of the 1976 All-America Rose Selections winner 'America', Climbing America carries the same warm coral-orange to salmon-pink, high-centered hybrid-tea-shaped blooms and rich spicy fragrance as its parent but on long, vigorous climbing canes that reach well up a trellis or arbor. It flowers in a strong spring flush with continued repeat bloom through summer and fall, making it a long-season source of color and cut flowers for a sunny fence line or entry arbor. Remove old, unproductive wood each winter to keep new flowering canes coming.

common_name: Blaze Climbing Rose (Improved Blaze Scarlet Climber)

planting.note: Set out own-root or grafted plants in spring or fall against a fence, mailbox post, or arbor in full sun; Blaze is an easy, forgiving climber for Gulf South gardens, tolerating average soil and less fastidious care than many modern climbing roses.

directions: Plant in full sun in well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and tie the vigorous canes in as they grow since Blaze climbs by producing long stems that must be trained rather than by twining on its own. Introduced in 1932 and improved with a stronger repeat-blooming selection released in the 1950s, Blaze became one of the most widely planted climbing roses in mid-20th-century America for its clusters of bright, semi-double scarlet-red blooms produced in a heavy spring flush with continued bloom through summer. It is exceptionally vigorous and forgiving, tolerating a wide range of soils and light care while still covering a fence or arbor with reliable color, which explains its enduring popularity in older Southern gardens. Prune out the oldest canes every couple of years at the base to keep the plant renewing itself with vigorous new growth.

common_name: William Baffin Rose (Cold-Hardy Explorer Series Climber)

planting.note: Set out own-root plants in spring or fall against a trellis, fence, or arbor in full sun; bred for extreme cold hardiness in Canada's Explorer series, William Baffin also performs reliably in warm Gulf South gardens thanks to its outstanding disease resistance and vigor.

directions: Plant in full sun in average, well-drained soil against a sturdy support, and expect vigorous growth that needs little more than occasional shaping once established. Bred by Agriculture Canada's Ogilvie/Svejda rose breeding program and introduced in 1983 as part of the cold-hardy Explorer series, William Baffin bears large clusters of semi-double, deep pink blooms with a light fragrance in a heavy spring flush and steady rebloom through summer and fall. Although developed for Canadian winters down to roughly zone 3, its outstanding vigor and near-immunity to blackspot and powdery mildew make it just as valuable in hot, humid Gulf South gardens, where many modern climbers struggle with disease pressure. Minimal pruning is needed beyond removing dead or crossing canes in late winter, since the plant blooms reliably on both old and new wood.
